title: Thinking with a document
excerpt: Giving AI a file to read and revise helped me carry better work from one run to the next. Writing it also made me clearer about what I was asking for.

sources.label: Rick's observation about documentation improving outputs across runs and agents, and article brief
Current shared collaboration principles: evidence, corrections, ownership, and original documents
Current Taskosaur work tracking and handoff guidance

intro: One of the more useful changes I made to working with AI was simple: I gave it a file to work on, then brought that file into the next run. The document held the problem, the decisions, and the corrections we needed to keep. Each session had something concrete to continue.

In my experience, the outputs became better across runs and across agents. I had a way to carry a correction forward instead of hoping it would survive in the chat. I also found that writing the document made me think more carefully about the work before asking an agent to do anything.

sections.heading: Writing exposes the parts I haven't figured out
body: An idea can feel clear in my head and still be difficult to explain. I might know a page feels confusing without knowing which decision needs to change. Writing helps me separate what I have observed from what I am assuming, then say what I want help with.

Imagine a request to make a project dashboard easier to use. That leaves a lot for an agent to guess. A more useful brief might say that a new user needs to find overdue work and understand who owns it without opening every project. Now there is a person, a task, and something to check. This is an illustrative example, but it captures the difference I am looking for when I write.

The next questions become easier to see. Should overdue work appear first? Does the user need a view of projects or people? Which part is a decision, and which part still needs exploration? A document lets me leave those questions visible while I work through them.

evidence.note: Rick requests a reflection on thinking with documentation. The dashboard example is explicitly illustrative, not an invented historical project.
Supports distinguishing observations, assumptions, and unresolved decisions.

sections.heading: Give corrections somewhere to go
body: A chat is useful for working through a response. I can push back, add context, or point out what feels wrong. But a correction has limited reach if the next session never sees it. I want the useful part of that exchange to change the starting point for future work.

If I explain that a section should focus on what a workspace enables, I can put that decision in the working document. The next agent can read the intent before rewriting the section. It still has to make good choices, but it has a clearer brief than the one I started with.

That is what I mean by giving AI a file to modify each run. The update should preserve what we learned, what we changed, and what remains open. There is no value in adding text just to prove that a run happened. Sometimes the right update is a correction or the removal of an instruction that no longer fits.

evidence.note: The reported cross-run benefit is Rick's observation. His earlier Portfolio feedback explicitly shifted the prototypes section toward what the workspace enables.
Current guidance belongs at its owner; replace stale rules rather than accumulating instructions.

sections.heading: Different agents can start from the same decisions
body: I move between Codex, Claude, Cursor, and Gemini. A document gives me a way to carry context between them without relying on each tool to remember the same conversations. That only works when the agent can access the document and actually reads the relevant parts.

I need one clear current version. If I copy the instructions into several places and revise only one, I have created a new source of confusion. Linking to the original makes it easier to know where a correction belongs and which version the next agent should use.

The tools can still interpret the same brief differently. What improves is the starting material: they can see the accepted decisions, the evidence, and the unfinished questions. I can compare their work against that shared reference instead of spending the whole exchange reconstructing context.

evidence.note: The conversation establishes use of several agents and Rick's reported improvement across them.
Requires authoritative originals and truthful access claims; no automatic cross-tool memory is implied.

sections.heading: The document gives me something to question
body: When an agent edits a document, I can inspect the change. Did it preserve the scope? Did it turn an assumption into a fact? Did it quietly drop a constraint because a different answer was easier to produce? Those questions are much easier to ask when I can compare the work with a written intention.

This helps my own thinking too. A polished response can move past a choice I have not made. Keeping that choice visible gives me time to compare alternatives and decide what I believe. The document becomes a place where I can revise my understanding as well as the agent's instructions.

I do not keep every exchange. I keep the parts someone needs to continue: the goal, relevant constraints, decisions and reasons, what has been checked, open questions, and the next useful action. That is usually more helpful than a long transcript.

evidence.note: Defines compact continuation context and meaningful checkpoints rather than transcript duplication.
Thinking benefits are reflective interpretation for Rick's review.

sections.heading: Read, work, check, update
body: The rhythm is straightforward. Start by reading the current document. Do the work against the goal and constraints it records. Check the result, including anything the agent claims is finished. Then revise the document so it reflects the decisions and evidence worth carrying into the next run.

That last step is the handoff. If something failed, record what failed and what still needs checking. If a decision changed, explain why. If another person or agent has edited the file in the meantime, reconcile their changes before saving over them. The next session needs an honest starting point, including the unfinished parts.

evidence.note: Supports fresh orientation, verification, explicit unfinished work, and handoff checkpoints.
Requires preserving other writers' work and verifying claims.

sections.heading: What I mean by better outputs
body: I have not measured this as a controlled comparison, and I would not promise that every run improves. A file can preserve a mistake just as easily as a useful decision. Stale context, conflicting instructions, and unnecessary detail can all make the next result worse. I still need to review the work and keep the document useful.

Editing a file does not retrain the model. It changes the context available when I ask it to work again. For me, the practical improvement is that a correction has somewhere to survive, an unfinished question remains visible, and the next agent can begin with more of what I already know.
That is a modest habit with a useful effect. I can think something through, make the reasoning visible, and leave the work in a state I can return to. The next conversation starts from there.

evidence.note: Qualitative personal experience only. No controlled benchmark, quantified gain, or guaranteed improvement is asserted.
Supports review, correction, and removal of stale guidance; document updates are context changes, not model training.
